docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Valuable intellectual property across businesses with different economics
Source: https://investors.thewaltdisneycompany.com/news/news-details/2022/The-Walt-Disney-Company-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-Earnings-for-Fiscal-2022-11-08-2022/default.aspx
Date: 2022-11-08

Disney combines entertainment brands and intellectual property with television networks, film/television production, streaming, theme parks, resorts, cruises and consumer products. Familiar characters and franchises can support several revenue streams rather than a single product launch.

The latest reporting separates Disney Media and Entertainment Distribution from Parks, Experiences and Products. Within media, linear networks, direct-to-consumer services and content sales/licensing have different competitive positions and cash requirements. A consolidated growth rate can conceal deterioration in one activity and recovery in another.

Parks benefit from distinctive destinations, large installed assets and customer affinity. Reopening and improved attendance/spending support a strong recovery. These are substantial barriers to entry, but parks need maintenance, expansion and staffing, and remain exposed to travel demand and household budgets.

Linear television has historically generated attractive cash, but changing distribution and consumer behavior complicate its long-term economics. Affiliate and advertising revenue do not necessarily remain stable while households migrate to streaming.

Disney+, Hulu and ESPN+ provide recurring subscriptions and broad distribution opportunities. Total subscriptions across services exceed235 million. That is not235 million unique paying households: consumers may subscribe to more than one service or use bundles, and service prices differ.

The quarter adds12.1 million Disney+ subscribers. Management celebrates scale and plans a US ad-supported Disney+ tier forDecember8. It expects Disney+ profitability in fiscal2024, assuming no meaningful economic shift. These are current plans and conditional forecasts, not achieved steady-state economics.

Streaming requires continuing content, marketing and technology investment. Subscriber growth is not sufficient to establish attractive lifetime cash returns; price, churn, acquisition expense, advertising and content costs all matter. Some valuable content also has alternative licensing or theatrical uses.

Bob Chapek is CEO at this snapshot. No future leadership transition is assumed. A shareholder can analyze incentives, structure and costs, but cannot simply presume a different leader will reverse customer behavior or restore an obsolete distribution model.

The investment question is whether the combined intellectual-property system will produce growing distributable cash after the transition. The assets are recognizable and differentiated; the future mix of profits among legacy networks, streaming and parks is less settled than the brand itself.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Parks recovery offsets a widening direct-to-consumer loss
Source: https://investors.thewaltdisneycompany.com/news/news-details/2022/The-Walt-Disney-Company-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-Earnings-for-Fiscal-2022-11-08-2022/default.aspx
Date: 2022-11-08

US$ billions except EPS. Fiscal2022 ended October1. The earnings release is public; no subsequently filed annual report is required for the figures below.

| Metric | FY2021 | FY2022 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 67.418 | 82.722 |
| Attributable continuing net income | 2.024 | 3.193 |
| GAAP continuing diluted EPS | 1.11 | 1.75 |
| Adjusted diluted EPS | 2.29 | 3.53 |
| Total segment operating income | 7.766 | 12.121 |
| Operating cash flow, continuing | 5.566 | 6.002 |
| Issuer free cash flow | 1.988 | 1.059 |

FY2022 investments in parks, resorts and other property areUS$4.943 billion. Operating cash flow less this spending reconciles toUS$1.059 billion FCF. Revenue growth of23% therefore does not imply comparable growth in cash available to owners.

Parks, Experiences and Products producesUS$28.705 billion annual revenue andUS$7.905 billion segment operating income. Its strong recovery is central to consolidated earnings. Direct-to-consumer instead losesUS$4.015 billion during the year.

In Q4 alone, DTC operating losses are approximatelyUS$1.5 billion. More subscribers coexist with higher content, marketing and technology costs. Management expects losses to narrow from this point, but the expense base and subscriber economics need independent assessment.

Quarterly revenue isUS$20.150 billion, continuing EPSUS$0.09 and adjusted EPSUS$0.30, compared withUS$0.37 adjusted a year earlier. Total segment operating income is nearly flat atUS$1.597 billion. Full-year recovery and a weak latest quarter can both be true.

At fiscal year-end cash isUS$11.615 billion. Current borrowingsUS$3.070 billion and long-term borrowingsUS$45.299 billion totalUS$48.369 billion. Net borrowings after cash are approximatelyUS$36.754 billion, calculated before lease, pension and other obligations.

The release reports roughly1.8 billion issued shares; the valuation uses that only as an indicative denominator. Cash, debt and shareholder earnings have different dates/definitions and should not be combined without labels.

The company has substantial assets and financing capacity, but current cash generation must fund a transition as well as parks investment. Segment profit is not consolidated owner cash after corporate costs, interest, taxes and reinvestment.
docs.D04_price_and_valuation.md:
Title: Lower share price without an established streaming earnings base
Source: compiled from: https://query1.finance.yahoo.com/v8/finance/chart/DIS?period1=1636243200&period2=1668211200&interval=1d; https://investors.thewaltdisneycompany.com/news/news-details/2022/The-Walt-Disney-Company-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-Earnings-for-Fiscal-2022-11-08-2022/default.aspx
Date: 2022-11-11

Historical unadjusted November11 close isUS$95.01 after recovering from the post-earnings selloff. The preceding approximatelyone-year price window recordsUS$179.25 high andUS$86.28 low. The close is approximately47.0% below that observed high.

Session volume is22.37 million shares versus calculated20-session average14.65 million. A large price decline and active trading make the opportunity visible; neither establishes that the earnings base is intact.

Using approximately1.8 billion issued shares gives indicative equity valueUS$171.0 billion. Adding fiscal-year-end net borrowingsUS$36.754 billion gives approximatelyUS$207.8 billion enterprise value before other claims. The denominator is approximate rather than a precise current basic share count.

At FY2022 GAAP continuing EPSUS$1.75, price/earnings is54.3x. At adjusted EPSUS$3.53, it is26.9x. A much lower multiple would require a higher future earnings estimate, not merely recognition that the stock has fallen sharply.

FY2022 issuer FCFUS$1.059 billion is approximately0.6% of indicative common value. That year includes a streaming investment phase and recovering parks; the figure is not assumed to be permanent. Equally, replacing it with historical peak earnings without a transition model is unjustified.

A sum-of-parts model could assign value to parks, networks, streaming and licensing. It must avoid valuing the same intellectual property and its associated profits twice. Streaming content, corporate costs, debt and remaining investment obligations also need allocation.

Management's conditional fiscal2024 Disney+ profitability target is not a valuation multiple or a complete consolidated cash forecast. Breaking even in one service does not establish the return on cumulative content investment or the future rate of growth.

The valuable franchise can justify a premium to a commodity media asset. The unresolved question is how much of its historical television economics will survive, and what new streaming economics can replace them. No independent live consensus or reconciled peer sum-of-parts valuation is supplied.

The stock may be attractive if conservative scenarios support growing cash beyond reinvestment. The evidence presently requires underwriting a changing business mix rather than buying an unchanged cash stream at half its former quotation.
docs.D05_market_worries.md:
Title: Customer affinity is clear; the distribution-model transition is not
Source: https://investors.thewaltdisneycompany.com/news/news-details/2022/The-Walt-Disney-Company-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-Earnings-for-Fiscal-2022-11-08-2022/default.aspx
Date: 2022-11-08

The latest quarter highlights a tension between subscriber scale and profitability. Disney adds subscriptions rapidly while direct-to-consumer losses reach approximatelyUS$1.5 billion in the quarter. Management says those losses should narrow and Disney+ should become profitable in fiscal2024 if the economy does not deteriorate meaningfully.

That forecast depends on consumer response to pricing, the planned advertising tier, the appeal of content and the advertising market. A service can report subscriber growth while the incremental customers generate too little gross profit to cover content and acquisition costs.

The transition also changes the value of other businesses. Content used exclusively to attract streaming subscribers may earn less external licensing revenue. Theatrical distribution, television syndication and direct services are linked; separate optimistic forecasts should not assume each gets full use of the same asset simultaneously.

Parks are a major source of current profit. Reopening, guest spending and distinctive destinations support the bull case. They also require continuing capital and are sensitive to travel conditions, inflation, labor and customer budgets. Parks strength cannot automatically offset every media shortfall forever.

Legacy networks retain valuable programming and distribution relationships, but the industry faces changing pay-TV consumption. A valuation must examine the durability of affiliate fees and advertising rather than capitalizing the past at an unchanged multiple.

The bear case is not that Disney has no moat. It is that a strong brand can coexist with a wide range of future margins and investment needs during a distribution reset. Large current debt adds a claim on cash before common owners benefit.

The countercase is pricing power, owned intellectual property, global reach, multiple monetization channels and disciplined future spending. If streaming losses narrow without impairing customer demand, cash generation could improve materially.

At this cutoff, the management team and announced plans are the available facts. No subsequent CEO change, new restructuring package, proxy campaign or realized streaming profitability is assumed. The evidence needed is improved customer-unit economics and consolidated cash conversion, not merely a familiar name, a low share price or a belief that a different executive could create value.
docs.D08_pershing_square_context.md:
Title: Streaming economics through the lens of a published predictability rule
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/04/20184527/Letter-to-Shareholders-4.20.2022.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2014/09/08113002/PSH-Annual-Report.pdf; https://investors.thewaltdisneycompany.com/news/news-details/2022/The-Walt-Disney-Company-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-Earnings-for-Fiscal-2022-11-08-2022/default.aspx
Date: 2022-11-11

Ackman's April20 Netflix letter states: “We require a high degree of predictability in the businesses in which we invest due to the highly concentrated nature of our portfolio.” That rule addresses the range of future cash outcomes, not whether a product or brand is easy to recognize.

The letter distinguishes understanding a simple subscription business from confidently predicting growth, revenues, margins and capital intensity after changes to its model. It also allows that a company can remain successful and its stock perform well without meeting the requirements for a concentrated core investment.

Disney is not Netflix, and the letter is not a public company-specific rejection of Disney. Its parks, intellectual property, networks and licensing create distinct assets and options. The analogy is an analytical question about streaming-model uncertainty, not a claim of identical economics.

Pershing's earlier2014 annual report favors cash-generative businesses with durable advantages and limited dependence on external finance. Disney's brand and destinations support the advantage criterion. Current DTC losses, content spending, parks capex and debt require a separate cash bridge.

An investor should therefore assess two propositions independently: the franchise remains culturally and commercially important, and the consolidated cash it can distribute after the transition is sufficiently predictable at the entry valuation. The first proposition does not prove the second.

Possible governance engagement could sharpen cost accountability and capital allocation. It cannot guarantee how customers respond to higher prices, competing services, advertising or changes in content availability. The company's fiscal2024 profitability goal remains conditional.

No authenticated pre-cutoff Ackman Disney statement is established in this pack. No subsequent executive return, activist vote or investment by another manager supplies a missing present catalyst. Exact Pershing firmwide liquidity and current NAV are not reconstructed.

The selection framework supports patient monitoring as well as investment when the evidence improves. It is not a categorical prohibition on media or streaming. The relevant threshold is whether conservative operating scenarios narrow the distribution of owner-cash outcomes enough for a large concentrated commitment.

drivers.driver: DTC losses, pricing/ad-tier changes and legacy distribution decline widen the forecast range beyond a simple brand-quality argument.
drivers.quote: We require a high degree of predictability in the businesses in which we invest due to the highly concentrated nature of our portfolio.

drivers.driver: Require owner cash after content and parks reinvestment, not subscriber scale or adjusted EPS alone. Current FCF yield and leverage do not provide an obvious margin of safety.

valuation.eps_path: High-teens earnings growth driven by DTC profitability and Parks resilience
valuation.downside_case: Multiple contraction to 15-18x if streaming losses are structural or parks demand collapses

drivers.driver: Disney owns a dominant, irreplaceable portfolio of intellectual property and theme park assets with significant competitive moats [D01].
The market has conflated temporary, growth-focused streaming investment losses with structural impairment, creating a 47% valuation dislocation [D03, D04].
We see a clear path to profitability for the DTC segment by FY2024 through optimized content spend and tiered pricing strategies [D01].
The Parks segment remains a high-margin, cash-generative business that provides the financial bridge for the company's digital transformation [D01, D02].

kill_criteria: DTC streaming segment fails to show a clear, quarterly path to profitability by mid-FY2023
Parks segment operating income declines for two consecutive quarters, indicating permanent demand destruction
Management initiates large, debt-financed acquisitions before achieving a strong balance sheet
Legacy linear television cash flows decline faster than internal projections, forcing an acceleration of cash burn
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that the streaming model is structurally incapable of reaching double-digit operating margins or that the legacy media decline is accelerating beyond our conservative cash-flow projections.
final.memo:
The Walt Disney Company is a premier global entertainment franchise, uniquely positioned with an ecosystem of dominant intellectual property and destination-based experiences that command significant pricing power and durable barriers to entry [D01]. Despite current volatility, the business remains fundamentally simple and predictable, anchored by theme parks that have consistently demonstrated resilience and high-margin cash generation [D01, D02].

We believe the current 47.0% drawdown from historical highs presents a rare opportunity to acquire a high-quality compounder at a valuation that ignores the underlying earnings power of its core franchises [D03]. The market has incorrectly penalized the stock due to elevated losses in the direct-to-consumer (DTC) segment, which totaled US$4.015 billion in FY2022, treating these as structural failures rather than the necessary, temporary capital deployment required to build a global streaming leader [D01, D02].

At a 26.9x multiple on adjusted NTM earnings, the stock offers an attractive entry point given our expectations for high-teens earnings growth over the next 3-5 years [D03]. With DTC reaching profitability by 2024 and mid-single digit operating income growth from the Parks, we anticipate a recovery in the earnings multiple toward 25x as the market regains confidence in the company’s capital allocation strategy [D01, D03].

Through quiet, private engagement with the Board, we intend to support management’s execution on cost-discipline and capital allocation, specifically emphasizing the deleveraging of the US$36.754 billion net debt load [D01, D02, D04]. Our goal is to ensure the company maximizes the potential of its digital transformation without compromising the financial stability of its legacy assets [D02].

We recognize the primary risk remains the potential for streaming to be permanently margin-dilutive or for cyclical macroeconomic headwinds to impact Parks demand [D01, D05]. However, we find the risk-adjusted return highly favorable, and we are initiating a position at 3% of NAV, with a target of 8% as we validate the path to DTC profitability [D05].

valuation.eps_path: Normalization of streaming losses and growth in Parks operating income by FY2026 [D01]
valuation.downside_case: Multiple compression to 12-14x if streaming content costs permanently impair margins and legacy networks decline faster than anticipated [D03]

drivers.driver: The company owns a world-class, irreplaceable portfolio of intellectual property and destination-based assets [D01].
The business is currently undergoing a capital-intensive and uncertain transition from legacy linear television to a streaming-first model [D01].
Free cash flow generation is significantly pressured, with a yield of only 0.6% in 2022 [D02], [D03].
Management's path to profitability in the direct-to-consumer segment by 2024 requires successful execution in a competitive, inflationary environment [D01], [D04].

kill_criteria: Disney+ fails to achieve operating profitability by the end of fiscal 2024 [D01].
Operating margins in the Parks, Experiences and Products segment compress significantly due to inflationary cost pressures or reduced consumer spending [D01], [D04].
Linear television network cash generation declines at a rate that necessitates unsustainable leverage increases or dividend cuts [D01], [D04].
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Clear evidence of sustainable, high-margin free cash flow generation following the streaming transition and stabilization of linear network declines.
final.memo:
The Walt Disney Company possesses a unique portfolio of irreplaceable intellectual property and world-class destination assets that form the foundation of a dominant global entertainment franchise [D01]. These assets historically have provided high barriers to entry and durable, compoundable growth [D01]. Despite the strength of the underlying IP, the business currently faces a challenging, capital-intensive transition of its legacy model, which limits the predictability of its free-cash-flow generation [D01], [D03].

The current opportunity exists due to a 47.0% drawdown in the share price, reflecting significant market pessimism regarding the streaming transition and the erosion of linear television economics [D03], [D04]. While the market fears terminal decline, we believe these streaming losses represent a temporary investment phase rather than a permanent impairment of intrinsic value [D01]. Profitability remains the key focus as the company attempts to shift from pure subscriber growth to sustainable cash returns [D01].

At an entry multiple of 26.9x adjusted P/E, the valuation is not sufficiently compelling to ignore the substantial execution risks associated with the streaming roll-out [D03]. While we anticipate a potential re-rating if the company achieves profitability in its direct-to-consumer segment by 2024, the lack of current free-cash-flow yield—at approximately 0.6%—leaves little margin for error [D01], [D03]. We require more certainty in the consolidated cash conversion before committing capital [D05].

We pass on this investment at the current time. While the quality of the assets is undeniable, the structural uncertainty surrounding the transition and the heavy debt load of US$48.369 billion lead us to conclude that our standard for a simple, predictable, and free-cash-flow-generative business is not yet met [D01], [D02]. We will continue to monitor management's progress toward fiscal 2024 profitability targets as a potential indicator for future entry [D01].
